claim: In the dentate gyrus, granule cells are known to be morphologically diverse.
source: In the dentate gyrus – a key component of spatial memory circuits – granule cells (GCs) are known to be morphologically diverse and to display heterogeneous activity profiles during behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about dentate gyrus granule cells.

claim: Granule cells in the dentate gyrus display heterogeneous activity profiles during behavior.
source: In the dentate gyrus – a key component of spatial memory circuits – granule cells (GCs) are known to be morphologically diverse and to display heterogeneous activity profiles during behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about dentate gyrus granule cells.

claim: The vast majority of dentate gyrus granule cells were silent during exploration.
source: We found that the vast majority of neurons were silent during exploration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the juxtacellular recording experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: Most active granule cells displayed a characteristic spike waveform.
source: Most active GCs displayed a characteristic spike waveform, fired at low rates and showed spatial activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most active granule cells fired at low rates.
source: Most active GCs displayed a characteristic spike waveform, fired at low rates and showed spatial activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most active granule cells showed spatial activity.
source: Most active GCs displayed a characteristic spike waveform, fired at low rates and showed spatial activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Primary dendritic parameters were sufficient for classifying neurons as active or silent with high accuracy.
source: Primary dendritic parameters were sufficient for classifying neurons as active or silent with high accuracy.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the morphological analysis and machine learning classification reported in the manuscript.

claim: The data support a sparse coding scheme in the dentate gyrus.
source: Our data thus support a sparse coding scheme in the dentate gyrus and provide a possible link between structural and functional heterogeneity among the GC population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The data provide a possible link between structural and functional heterogeneity among the granule cell population.
source: Our data thus support a sparse coding scheme in the dentate gyrus and provide a possible link between structural and functional heterogeneity among the GC population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sparse activity is a hallmark feature of cortical and hippocampal function.
source: Sparse activity is a hallmark feature of cortical and hippocampal function (Treves and Rolls, 1994; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Wolfe et al., 2010; Barth and Poulet, 2012; Spanne and Jörntell, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In neocortical circuits, sparse representations are thought to be crucial for optimal encoding of sensory stimuli.
source: In neocortical circuits, sparse representations are thought to be crucial for optimal encoding of sensory stimuli (Brecht et al., 2004; Huber et al., 2008; Li et al., 2009; Rochefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In hippocampal circuits, the skewed distribution of population firing activity indicates that a preconfigured, highly active minority of neurons dominates information coding.
source: Similarly in hippocampal circuits, the skewed distribution of population firing activity indicates that a preconfigured, highly active minority of neurons dominates information coding (Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013; Buzsaki and Mizuseki, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The dentate gyrus is among the most sparse networks known to date.
source: The dentate gyrus (DG) is among the most sparse networks known to date.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Extracellular recordings in foraging rodents have revealed that only a tiny minority of putative granule cells is active during behavior, while the rest are silent.
source: Extracellular recordings in foraging rodents have in fact revealed that only a tiny minority of principal neurons – putative granule cells (GCs) – is active during behavior, while the rest are silent (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous extracellular recording studies.

claim: The cellular identity of active and silent neurons in the dentate gyrus has remained largely unexplored.
source: Although several structure–function schemes have been proposed (Leutgeb et al., 2007; Alme et al., 2010; Lisman, 2011; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014), the cellular identity of active and silent neurons has remained largely unexplored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: An advantage of juxtacellular recording over conventional extracellular methods is that neurons can be identified irrespective of their spiking activity.
source: An advantage of this technique over conventional extracellular methods is that neurons can be identified irrespective of their spiking activity; thus, both silent and active cells can be sampled during free behavior (i.e. under intact sensory, motor and vestibular inputs), which enables the analysis of sparsely active networks (Hromádka et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2010; Herfst et al., 2012; Burgalossi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage and supported by citations to previous work using this technique.

claim: Juxtacellular recording enables both silent and active cells to be sampled during free behavior.
source: An advantage of this technique over conventional extracellular methods is that neurons can be identified irrespective of their spiking activity; thus, both silent and active cells can be sampled during free behavior (i.e. under intact sensory, motor and vestibular inputs), which enables the analysis of sparsely active networks (Hromádka et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2010; Herfst et al., 2012; Burgalossi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Active granule cells displayed morphological features of mature granule cells.
source: This neuron displayed morphological features of mature GCs (see Materials and methods and Figure 1A) and discharged sparsely during the awake state (average firing rate=0.49 Hz; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of identified neurons shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A spontaneously active granule cell discharged sparsely during the awake state with an average firing rate of 0.49 Hz.
source: This neuron displayed morphological features of mature GCs (see Materials and methods and Figure 1A) and discharged sparsely during the awake state (average firing rate=0.49 Hz; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from an identified neuron shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spikes from active granule cells displayed a 'shoulder' following the positive peak of the juxtacellular spike.
source: Notably, spikes from this neuron displayed a 'shoulder' following the positive peak of the juxtacellular spike, which was best evident as a local maximum in the first derivative of the juxtacellular voltage trace (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The spike shoulder was best evident as a local maximum in the first derivative of the juxtacellular voltage trace.
source: Notably, spikes from this neuron displayed a 'shoulder' following the positive peak of the juxtacellular spike, which was best evident as a local maximum in the first derivative of the juxtacellular voltage trace (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a methodological observation about how spike shoulders were detected, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 47 active neurons were recorded and identified during urethane theta-oscillations (n=19), awake head-fixation (n=4) and free-behavior (n=24).
source: Altogether, we recorded and identified 47 active neurons during urethane theta-oscillations (n=19), awake head-fixation (n=4) and free-behavior (n=24) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental dataset shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All neurons displaying spike-shoulders were located within the granule cell layer, with the exception of one excitatory neuron just below the granule cell layer.
source: Irrespective of the recording condition (i.e. anesthetized versus awake), we found that all neurons displaying spike-shoulders were located within the GC layer (n=17; with the exception of one excitatory neuron just below the GC layer; see Figure 1D,E and Materials and methods) and corresponded to morphologically mature GCs (see criteria in Materials and methods; n=15 cases where morphology could be assessed).
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization of recorded neurons shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Neurons displaying spike-shoulders corresponded to morphologically mature granule cells in 15 cases where morphology could be assessed.
source: Irrespective of the recording condition (i.e. anesthetized versus awake), we found that all neurons displaying spike-shoulders were located within the GC layer (n=17; with the exception of one excitatory neuron just below the GC layer; see Figure 1D,E and Materials and methods) and corresponded to morphologically mature GCs (see criteria in Materials and methods; n=15 cases where morphology could be assessed).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of identified neurons.

claim: In CA3c, fast-spiking, and hilar neurons, spike-shoulders were not identified.
source: In CA3c (n=7), fast-spiking (n=10) and hilar (n=17) neurons, spike-shoulders were not identified (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike waveforms from different neuron types shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Spike-shoulders from granule cells resulted in a relatively long duration of the juxtacellular spike signal.
source: In most cases spike-shoulders from GCs were already apparent in the average spike waveform (Figure 1C,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and resulted in a relatively long duration of the juxtacellular spike signal (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike waveform characteristics shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Recordings could be assigned to the granule cell class based solely on the average spike waveforms with approximately 89% accuracy.
source: Furthermore, recordings could be assigned with high accuracy to the GC class based solely on the average spike waveforms (~89%; cross-validated; see Materials and methods for details), thus providing additional evidence for a correlation between spike-shoulders and GC identity.
evidence: This is based on machine learning classification analysis of spike waveforms.

claim: Of 190 juxtacellular recordings established in the granule cell layer, 163 were from silent neurons.
source: Of 190 juxtacellular recordings established in the GC layer, 163 were from silent neurons (see Materials and methods and Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental dataset shown in Figure 2.

claim: Silent granule cells did not fire during exploration.
source: Both neurons displayed morphological features of mature GCs (Figure 2A,C) and did not fire during exploration (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is based on recordings from identified silent neurons shown in Figure 2.

claim: Spiking in silent granule cells was readily induced by current injection.
source: Spiking was readily induced by current injection (Figure 2E), which was used in a subset of cases to label the neurons at the end of the recording session (see Materials and methods; Pinault, 1996; Herfst et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is based on experimental manipulation shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Active granule cells accounted for only approximately 14% (27 out of 190) of all neurons sampled within the granule cell layer.
source: Active GCs were thus very sparse and accounted for only ~14% (27 out of 190) of all neurons sampled within the GC layer (Figure 2F; we note that this is likely to represent an overestimate, since silent juxtacellular 'hits' were often discarded; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the experimental dataset shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The proportion of active granule cells (14%) is likely to represent an overestimate, since silent juxtacellular 'hits' were often discarded.
source: Active GCs were thus very sparse and accounted for only ~14% (27 out of 190) of all neurons sampled within the GC layer (Figure 2F; we note that this is likely to represent an overestimate, since silent juxtacellular 'hits' were often discarded; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an inference about potential bias in the sampling method.

claim: Nine spontaneously active granule cells were successfully labeled and identified in freely moving animals.
source: Nine spontaneously active GCs were successfully labeled and identified in freely moving animals; consistent with previous observations (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996), the sharpest spatial activity was observed within the subset of neurons displaying highest firing rates (>1 Hz); two of these neurons are shown in Figure 3A–H.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental dataset shown in Figure 3.

claim: The sharpest spatial activity was observed within the subset of neurons displaying highest firing rates (>1 Hz).
source: Nine spontaneously active GCs were successfully labeled and identified in freely moving animals; consistent with previous observations (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996), the sharpest spatial activity was observed within the subset of neurons displaying highest firing rates (>1 Hz); two of these neurons are shown in Figure 3A–H.
evidence: This is based on analysis of spatial firing patterns and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: A large fraction of spikes from an identified granule cell occurred within bursts.
source: A large fraction of spikes (Figure 3C) occurred within bursts (Figure 3D; see also Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014) and was rhythmically entrained by local field potential (LFP) theta oscillations (4–12Hz; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike timing shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Spikes from an identified granule cell were rhythmically entrained by local field potential theta oscillations (4–12Hz).
source: A large fraction of spikes (Figure 3C) occurred within bursts (Figure 3D; see also Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014) and was rhythmically entrained by local field potential (LFP) theta oscillations (4–12Hz; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike-LFP relationships shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Close anatomical proximity (< 1 µm; compatible with putative synaptic contacts) was observed between mossy boutons and large hilar neurons (4 out of 13 analyzed boutons).
source: Close anatomical proximity (< 1 µm; compatible with putative synaptic contacts) was observed between mossy boutons and large hilar neurons (4 out of 13 analyzed boutons; not shown), suggesting that hilar neurons might integrate spatial signals from upstream GCs.
evidence: This is based on anatomical analysis of labeled neurons.

claim: Hilar neurons might integrate spatial signals from upstream granule cells.
source: Close anatomical proximity (< 1 µm; compatible with putative synaptic contacts) was observed between mossy boutons and large hilar neurons (4 out of 13 analyzed boutons; not shown), suggesting that hilar neurons might integrate spatial signals from upstream GCs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on anatomical observations.

claim: 27 active granule cells (9 identified and 18 classified) were recorded during spatial exploration.
source: Altogether, we recorded 27 active GCs (9 identified and 18 classified) during spatial exploration.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental dataset.

claim: Most but not all identified active granule cells displayed spike-shoulders (18 out of 21; approximately 86%).
source: We note that since most but not all identified active GCs displayed spike-shoulders (18 out of 21; ~86%, Figure 1D), a fraction of GC recordings (~14%) is likely to be misclassified as false-negative in our dataset.
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike waveforms from identified neurons.

claim: A fraction of granule cell recordings (approximately 14%) is likely to be misclassified as false-negative in the dataset.
source: We note that since most but not all identified active GCs displayed spike-shoulders (18 out of 21; ~86%, Figure 1D), a fraction of GC recordings (~14%) is likely to be misclassified as false-negative in our dataset.
evidence: This is an inference about classification accuracy based on the observed data.

claim: In the majority of cases, firing occurred at single spatial locations (8 out of 11 recordings).
source: In line with the examples shown in Figure 3, in the majority of cases firing occurred at single spatial locations (8 out of 11 recordings; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; see details in Materials and methods), suggesting that these spatial firing patterns are likely to arise from the mature GC population (Danielson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spatial firing patterns shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spatial firing patterns with single firing fields are likely to arise from the mature granule cell population.
source: In line with the examples shown in Figure 3, in the majority of cases firing occurred at single spatial locations (8 out of 11 recordings; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; see details in Materials and methods), suggesting that these spatial firing patterns are likely to arise from the mature GC population (Danielson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Seven silent and six active granule cells were reconstructed for morphological analysis.
source: To this end, we first reconstructed the somato-dendritic compartment of seven silent and six active GCs (all of which were classified as morphologically mature; see Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and criteria in Materials and methods), which were selected for the morphological analysis on the basis of their high-quality filling (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the morphological analysis dataset shown in Figure 4.

claim: All reconstructed granule cells were classified as morphologically mature.
source: To this end, we first reconstructed the somato-dendritic compartment of seven silent and six active GCs (all of which were classified as morphologically mature; see Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and criteria in Materials and methods), which were selected for the morphological analysis on the basis of their high-quality filling (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on morphological criteria applied to reconstructed neurons.

claim: A logistic regression classifier was able to distinguish active and silent cells with good accuracy (approximately 85%, 11 out of 13 cells classified correctly).
source: The classifier was able to distinguish active and silent cells with good accuracy independent of the enforced level of sparsity (leave-one-out cross-validation accuracy ~85%, 11 out of 13 cells classified correctly).
evidence: This is based on machine learning classification analysis of morphological features.

claim: The classification accuracy was significantly higher than chance (p=0.03).
source: This classification accuracy was significantly higher than chance (p=0.03, permutation test, 500 runs, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of the classification results.

claim: Longer high-order dendrites (5 and 6 orders) were most predictive of active cells.
source: Overall, longer high-order dendrites (5 and 6 orders) were most predictive of active cells, whereas shorter low-order dendrites (2 and 3 orders) together with a higher number of primary dendrites were most predictive of silent cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of classifier weights shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Shorter low-order dendrites (2 and 3 orders) together with a higher number of primary dendrites were most predictive of silent cells.
source: Overall, longer high-order dendrites (5 and 6 orders) were most predictive of active cells, whereas shorter low-order dendrites (2 and 3 orders) together with a higher number of primary dendrites were most predictive of silent cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of classifier weights shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The morphological differences between active and silent neurons were unlikely to have resulted from methodological or procedural biases.
source: Notably, the morphological differences between active and silent neurons (Figure 4A,B) were unlikely to have resulted from methodological or procedural biases (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This is based on control analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the dataset of identified neurons (n=13), dendritic architectures can be predictive of granule cell activity during behavior.
source: This indicates that in our dataset of identified neurons (n=13), dendritic architectures can be predictive of GC activity during behavior (see also Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological classification analysis.

claim: Sparse coding in the dentate gyrus has been postulated to subserve 'pattern separation', a key function during memory processing.
source: Sparse coding in the DG has been postulated to subserve 'pattern separation', a key function during memory processing (McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Myers and Scharfman, 2009; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: The large majority of juxtacellularly sampled neurons within the granule cell layer are silent during exploration.
source: Here we show that indeed the large majority of juxtacellularly sampled neurons within the GC layer are silent during exploration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The small fraction of active granule cells displayed characteristic juxtacellular spike waveforms, characterized by the presence of 'shoulders' following the positive action potential peak.
source: The small fraction of active GCs (Figure 2F) displayed characteristic juxtacellular spike waveforms, characterized by the presence of 'shoulders' following the positive action potential peak (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Spike-shoulders served as a reliable correlate of granule cell identity.
source: Although, at present, we ignore the relative contributions of capacitive and/or ionic mechanisms to spike-shoulders, they served as a reliable correlate of GC identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between spike-shoulders and identified granule cells.

claim: If spike-shoulder waveform signatures can be resolved extracellularly, they could be instrumental for future classification of tetrode-recorded dentate gyrus units.
source: If such waveform signatures can also be resolved extracellularly – which remains to be demonstrated – they could be instrumental for future classification of tetrode-recorded DG units.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future applications of the findings.

claim: The study provides direct anatomical evidence that morphologically mature granule cells can display spatial firing.
source: We also provide direct anatomical evidence that morphologically mature GCs can display spatial firing, which in most cases occurred at single spatial locations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on combined morphological and electrophysiological data from identified neurons.

claim: The limited recording durations and spatial sampling prevent rigorous comparison with previous extracellular studies.
source: Although this is consistent with previous work (Leutgeb et al., 2007; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012), the limited recording durations and spatial sampling prevent rigorous comparison with previous extracellular studies.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study.

claim: Recordings in large open-field environments will be required to resolve whether different firing patterns (single versus multiple firing fields) are contributed by distinct cell types within the dentate gyrus.
source: Recordings in large open-field environments will be required to resolve whether different firing patterns (single versus multiple firing fields) are contributed by distinct cell types within the DG (Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments to address remaining questions.

claim: Cell intrinsic and synaptic mechanisms can be major determinants of single-cell activity in sparsely active networks.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that cell intrinsic and synaptic mechanisms can be major determinants of single-cell activity in sparsely active networks (Crochet et al., 2011; Epsztein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The dendritic architecture of mature granule cells can be predictive of in-vivo spiking activity.
source: Our data indicate that the dendritic architecture of mature GCs can be predictive of in-vivo spiking activity (Figure 4D), thus providing a possible structure–function scheme for active and silent neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the morphological classification analysis.

claim: In the limited dataset of identified granule cells (n=13), structure–function relationships are subtle, as they derive from the combined analysis of multiple structural parameters.
source: We note, however, that in our limited dataset of identified GCs (n=13) structure–function relationships are subtle, as they derive from the combined analysis of multiple structural parameters (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the complexity and limitations of the morphological findings.

claim: Future work involving targeted manipulations of dendritic structures will be required to resolve the causal contribution of granule cell dendritic architectures to spatial representations.
source: Future work – possibly involving targeted manipulations of dendritic structures – will be required to resolve the causal contribution of GC dendritic architectures to spatial representations.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments to establish causality.

claim: The efficiency of juxtacellular filling was very similar between active and silent neurons (active, 6/14 labeling attempts, approximately 42%; silent, 7/19 labeling attempts, approximately 37%).
source: First, the efficiency of juxtacellular filling was very similar between active and silent neurons (active, 6/14 labeling attempts, ~42%; silent, 7/19 labeling attempts, ~37%).
evidence: This is based on quantification of labeling success rates.

claim: No apparent bias was observed in the distribution of active and silent neurons across animals.
source: Second, no apparent bias was observed in the distribution of active and silent neurons across animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and no correlation was observed between in-vivo activity and soma location within the GC layer or the laminar location of the cells (suprapyramidal versus infrapyramidal blade) (see Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the distribution of recordings across animals shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No correlation was observed between in-vivo activity and soma location within the granule cell layer.
source: Second, no apparent bias was observed in the distribution of active and silent neurons across animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and no correlation was observed between in-vivo activity and soma location within the GC layer or the laminar location of the cells (suprapyramidal versus infrapyramidal blade) (see Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of soma locations relative to activity status.

claim: No correlation was observed between in-vivo activity and the laminar location of the cells (suprapyramidal versus infrapyramidal blade).
source: Second, no apparent bias was observed in the distribution of active and silent neurons across animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and no correlation was observed between in-vivo activity and soma location within the GC layer or the laminar location of the cells (suprapyramidal versus infrapyramidal blade) (see Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of laminar locations relative to activity status.

claim: The quality of cell filling and dendritic labeling was similar between active and silent neurons.
source: Third, the quality of cell filling and dendritic labeling was similar between active and silent neurons.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of labeling quality shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dendritic complexity was not correlated to the labeling/filling quality (p=0.32; n=13).
source: Moreover, dendritic complexity was not correlated to the labeling/filling quality (p=0.32; n=13).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between dendritic complexity and labeling quality.

claim: The identified neurons are likely to represent a random sample of active and silent granule cells.
source: Altogether,these analyses indicate that our identified neurons are likely to represent a random sample of active and silent GCs, and that labeling biases are unlikely to account for the differences in morphological parameters between the two classes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control analyses performed.

claim: Labeling biases are unlikely to account for the differences in morphological parameters between active and silent granule cells.
source: Altogether,these analyses indicate that our identified neurons are likely to represent a random sample of active and silent GCs, and that labeling biases are unlikely to account for the differences in morphological parameters between the two classes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control analyses performed.

claim: Entry into the dentate gyrus molecular layer was always associated with a drastic increase in field-potential gamma oscillatory activity during exploratory behavior or urethane/ketamine anesthesia.
source: Entry into the DG (i.e. the molecular layer) was always associated with a drastic increase in field-potential gamma oscillatory activity during exploratory behavior or urethane/ketamine anesthesia.
evidence: This is a description of electrophysiological landmarks used for targeting.

claim: The beginning of the granule cell layer could be easily mapped because the entry into the densely packed cell layer was associated with an increase in the electrode resistance.
source: The beginning of the GC layer could always be easily mapped because the entry into the densely packed cell layer was associated with an increase in the electrode resistance (which was indicative of cell-contact).
evidence: This is a description of electrophysiological landmarks used for targeting.

claim: Multiple juxtacellular hits/recordings were typically established within the granule cell layer upon progressively advancing the electrode.
source: Multiple juxtacellular hits/recordings were typically established within the layer upon progressively advancing the electrode.
evidence: This is a description of the recording procedure.

claim: Entry into the hilar region was associated with a drop in the electrode resistance, which typically returned to its initial value.
source: Entry into the hilar region was associated with a drop in the electrode resistance, which typically returned to its initial value.
evidence: This is a description of electrophysiological landmarks used for targeting.

claim: Electrode resistance, LFP gamma oscillations and juxtacellular hit-rates served as reliable correlates of the electrode location within the granule cell layer.
source: Thus electrode resistance, LFP gamma oscillations and juxtacellular hit-rates served as reliable correlates of the electrode location within the GC layer.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the reliability of electrophysiological landmarks for targeting.

claim: Cell identification or anatomical verification of recording sites were in agreement with the expected electrode location.
source: Indeed, cell identification or anatomical verification of recording sites were in agreement with the expected electrode location.
evidence: This is a validation of the targeting approach based on post-hoc anatomical verification.

claim: All GCs recorded and identified in freely moving animals, for which morphology could be assessed (n=13), were classified as morphologically mature neurons.
source: All GCs recorded and identified in freely moving animals, for which morphology could be assessed (n=13; Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1), were classified as morphologically mature neurons according to previously established criteria; for example, based on their location within the GC layer, the absence of basal dendrites, the complex cone-shape of the dendritic arbor and, in the few cases where axons were recovered (e.g. Figure 3A), the presence of long-range axons and mossy boutons (Ambrogini et al., 2004; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004; Espósito et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2006; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: This is based on morphological criteria from previous literature applied to the reconstructed neurons.

claim: The few cells located within the lower third of the granule cell layer (n=3) were tested for doublecortin expression and were negative.
source: The few cells located within the lower third of the GC layer (n=3; of which two were silent and one active; see Figure 4—source data 1) were tested for doublecortin expression and were negative (not shown).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical testing of identified neurons.

claim: The result that cells in the lower third of the granule cell layer were doublecortin-negative is in line with the expected small proportion (approximately 5%) of morphologically immature GCs relative to the total GC population in young adult rats.
source: This result is in line with the expected small proportion (~5%) of morphologically immature GCs relative to the total GC population in young adult rats (Cameron and McKay, 2001; Gould, 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the doublecortin results in the context of previous literature.
